passages.title: City Unveils 14-Kilometre Cycle Network on Its Busiest Roads
paragraphs: A mid-sized city in north-eastern Thailand last week opened its first network of protected cycle lanes, physically separating bicycles from motor traffic with a raised concrete kerb along 14 kilometres of its busiest roads. Municipal officials say the 60-million-baht scheme is designed to make cycling feel safe not only for confident commuters but also for schoolchildren, older residents and first-time riders.

The project was prompted by a two-year review of local accident records, which found that cyclists and pedestrians accounted for nearly a third of road deaths in the city, even though they made up only about one in ten trips. Supporters also highlight the public health benefits of regular cycling, including lower rates of obesity and heart disease, and argue that fewer cars would reduce residents' exposure to exhaust fumes in congested districts.

Not everyone, however, is convinced. Shop owners along the central market road complain that the new lanes have eliminated around 200 roadside parking spaces, and they fear that customers who usually arrive by car will simply shop elsewhere. “Most of our buyers do not come on bicycles,” said one fabric seller, who asked not to be named.

City planners acknowledge that such worries are understandable but suggest they may prove unfounded, noting that similar schemes abroad have often increased the number of shoppers passing by. They will monitor sales and traffic flows for twelve months and have promised to create short-stay parking on side streets if trade declines significantly.

passages.title: Graduate Research Scholarships 2027
paragraphs: The Graduate School invites applications for its 2027 Graduate Research Scholarships, which support master's and doctoral research addressing health, environmental or social challenges in the Mekong region. Up to fifteen awards will be made this year.

Eligibility: Applicants must be enrolled full-time in a graduate programme at the university, and their research proposal must have been approved by their programme committee before the closing date. Students in their final semester, as well as those already holding a full scholarship from another source, are not eligible. Applicants need not be Thai nationals.

Value: Master's students will receive 120,000 baht and doctoral students 250,000 baht, paid in two instalments: 60 per cent upon signing the award agreement and the remainder once a satisfactory progress report has been accepted. Funds may cover fieldwork, laboratory materials and conference travel, but not tuition fees or personal equipment such as laptops.

Required documents: A complete application comprises (1) the online application form, (2) a research proposal of no more than ten pages, (3) an official transcript and (4) a letter of support from the principal supervisor. Evidence of English proficiency is required only where the project involves an overseas partner institution.

Deadline and selection: Applications close at 4:30 p.m. on 15 January 2027; late or incomplete submissions will not be considered. A panel of senior academics will shortlist candidates on the basis of academic merit and the potential impact of the proposed research. Shortlisted applicants will be invited to a fifteen-minute interview in late February, and results will be announced by 31 March. Enquiries should be directed to the Graduate School's research office.

passages.title: Pharmacists Welcome Plan as Survey Finds Metals in Supplements
paragraphs: Herbal medicines and dietary supplements will face considerably stricter controls under draft rules published this week by a national medicines regulator in Southeast Asia. If adopted, the rules would oblige manufacturers to demonstrate that their products meet basic quality standards before they reach pharmacy shelves, rather than after problems have been reported.

At present, most such products are registered on the basis of documents supplied by the manufacturers themselves, and only a small fraction are ever tested independently. Officials admit that this system has allowed substandard products to circulate for months before being withdrawn. In a recent market survey of 300 supplements carried out by a university laboratory, roughly one sample in eight contained heavy metals such as lead or arsenic above permitted limits, while several “natural” slimming capsules were found to contain prescription drugs that were not declared on the label.

Labelling is a second target. Under the proposals, packaging would have to list every active ingredient together with its quantity, and claims that a product can “cure” or “prevent” a disease would be prohibited unless backed by clinical evidence. Products would also have to carry warnings about possible interactions with conventional medicines; St John's wort, for instance, can reduce the effectiveness of some blood thinners and contraceptive pills.

Pharmacists have broadly welcomed the plan. “Patients often assume that anything herbal is harmless, so many never mention to their doctor what they are taking,” said Dr. Nattaya Sombat, a hospital pharmacist. “Clearer labels would make those conversations much easier and, frankly, safer.”

Some producers of traditional remedies, however, warn that the cost of laboratory testing could drive small family businesses out of the market. “Our recipes have been trusted for generations, and they deserve different treatment from factory-made chemicals,” said the owner of one such business. In response to these concerns, regulators have proposed a three-year transition period and subsidised testing for small manufacturers.

passages.title: Home, Office or Somewhere in Between?
paragraphs: When offices emptied during the COVID-19 pandemic, many managers predicted that productivity would collapse. Several years on, the evidence paints a far more complicated picture — one in which the answer depends on the type of work involved, the way remote arrangements are designed and how productivity is measured in the first place.

Some of the most encouraging findings come from studies of routine tasks whose output is easy to count. In one experiment at an insurance company, staff who processed claims from home completed about 8 per cent more cases per week than colleagues who remained in the office. The researchers attributed much of the gain to fewer interruptions and to the time saved on commuting, which some employees reinvested in their work.

Research on collaborative and creative work, by contrast, has produced less flattering results. An analysis of messaging data from several thousand employees at a software firm found that, once the company went fully remote, staff communicated mainly with their immediate teammates and far less with colleagues in other departments. Because new ideas often emerge from such informal contact across groups, the researchers warned that the damage might take years to become visible — long after short-term output figures had been reported.

Hybrid models, in which employees spend two or three days a week in the office, are increasingly presented as a compromise. A 2024 survey of 2,000 employees at mid-sized firms in Thailand and Malaysia found that hybrid workers reported higher job satisfaction than either fully remote or fully office-based staff, and that they were noticeably less likely to plan to leave their jobs. Managers' ratings of their performance, meanwhile, showed no significant difference.

Measurement itself remains a major obstacle. In many professional jobs, output cannot be reduced to a single number, so managers tend to rely on what they can observe — who arrives early and who stays late. Remote employees may therefore be judged less favourably even when they accomplish just as much. Conversely, employees' own estimates of their productivity are often more generous than those of their supervisors, and longer working hours at home can mean that total output rises while output per hour falls.

“Asking whether remote work is good or bad for productivity is like asking whether meetings are good or bad,” says Dr. Kanokwan Prasert, a labour economist. “The real question is which tasks, which people and which kind of arrangement.”

passages.title: Beyond the Clinic: Noncommunicable Diseases and National Development
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, heart disease, cancer, diabetes and chronic lung disease were regarded as the price of prosperity — conditions that afflicted the elderly populations of wealthy nations once infectious diseases had been brought under control. That view is now badly outdated. Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) have become the leading cause of death worldwide, and their burden is growing fastest in low- and middle-income countries, many of which are still struggling with tuberculosis, malaria and other infections. This article argues that NCDs should be understood not only as a medical problem but as an economic one, and that money spent on preventing them is better described as an investment than as a cost.

The scale of the problem is difficult to overstate. NCDs account for roughly seven in every ten deaths globally, and a substantial proportion of these are classified as premature, meaning that they occur before the age of 70. Contrary to the old stereotype, most premature NCD deaths now occur in low- and middle-income countries, where populations are ageing rapidly and where diets, working patterns and levels of physical activity have changed dramatically within a single generation. Epidemiologists describe the long-term shift from a pattern of illness dominated by infections to one dominated by chronic conditions as the epidemiological transition. In many countries, however, this transition remains incomplete, so health systems must cope with both burdens at once.

The most direct economic consequence is lost productivity. When a factory supervisor dies of a stroke at 52, or a teacher retires early because of kidney failure, the economy loses not only their current output but also skills and experience accumulated over decades. Illness also reduces the productivity of those who remain in work. Absenteeism — days taken off because of sickness or medical appointments — is relatively easy to record. Harder to detect, but often more costly, is presenteeism: the loss of output that occurs when employees come to work but perform below their normal capacity because of pain, fatigue or the side effects of treatment. A study of manufacturing workers in Southeast Asia, for example, estimated that presenteeism linked to poorly controlled diabetes cost employers almost twice as much as the sick days associated with the same condition.

For households, the burden is felt more immediately. Unlike an acute infection, which is typically treated within days or weeks, a chronic condition may require medication, monitoring and specialist care for the rest of a patient's life. Where health insurance is limited, these recurring expenses are paid largely out of pocket. Health economists use the term catastrophic health expenditure to describe spending that exceeds a set share of a household's capacity to pay, commonly 40 per cent of the income remaining after basic needs such as food have been met. Families facing such costs often resort to borrowing at high interest, selling land or livestock, or withdrawing children from school — choices that can trap them in poverty long after the patient has recovered or died. Moreover, the unpaid work of caring for a chronically ill relative falls disproportionately on women, many of whom reduce their working hours or leave paid employment altogether.

When these individual and household losses are added together, the macroeconomic picture becomes alarming. Chronic illness shrinks the labour force, reduces the savings that households would otherwise invest, and diverts public money from education and infrastructure towards long-term treatment. Modelling studies suggest that, over two decades, the cumulative output lost to the major NCDs in a typical middle-income economy could amount to a substantial fraction of a full year's gross domestic product. Countries with rapidly ageing populations, such as Thailand, are particularly exposed, because they will have proportionally fewer workers to support a growing number of people who need long-term care.

Against this background, prevention appears remarkably inexpensive. Many of the most effective measures operate at the level of the whole population rather than the individual patient: raising taxes on tobacco, alcohol and sugar-sweetened beverages; reducing the salt content of processed foods; restricting the marketing of unhealthy products to children; and designing cities in which walking and cycling are safe and convenient. Such policies cost governments relatively little to implement, and taxes actually generate revenue. One modelling exercise covering several Asian countries estimated that every dollar invested in a package of such measures could yield between five and ten dollars in economic benefits over fifteen years, largely through longer and healthier working lives.

Why, then, do governments continue to underinvest in prevention? Part of the explanation lies in the nature of the benefits themselves. A heart attack that never happens does not appear in any hospital record, and the savings it represents are spread across many years and many budgets. Political leaders, by contrast, are judged on visible achievements within short electoral cycles, and a new hospital wing is far easier to celebrate than a gradual decline in average blood pressure. Industries whose profits depend on tobacco, alcohol or processed food also lobby vigorously against regulation. Finally, ministries of finance have traditionally classified health spending as consumption rather than investment, so prevention competes for funds with every other form of current expenditure.

Overcoming these obstacles will require a change in the way NCDs are framed and measured. If governments routinely calculated the long-term returns of prevention — in productivity, tax revenue and avoided household poverty — the case for action would become far harder to ignore. Health ministries cannot achieve this alone; agriculture, trade, transport and education policies all shape the conditions in which chronic diseases develop. Treating NCD prevention as a shared, cross-government investment rather than as a narrow health expense may therefore be the most important step that countries can take to protect both the well-being of their citizens and the prosperity of their economies.

passages.title: Southeast Asia at an Energy Crossroads: Renewables in a Fast-Growing Region
paragraphs: Few regions illustrate the dilemmas of the global energy transition as clearly as Southeast Asia. Rising incomes, urbanisation and industrial growth have made it one of the fastest-growing sources of electricity demand in the world, and most of that demand is still met by burning coal and natural gas. At the same time, the region is exceptionally vulnerable to climate change, from rising seas in its crowded river deltas to stronger tropical storms. It also possesses abundant renewable resources: strong sunshine throughout the year, promising offshore wind sites and, in some countries, considerable geothermal and hydropower potential. This article argues that the main barriers to a faster transition are no longer technological but institutional — they lie in grids, finance and the fair distribution of costs and benefits.

Solar power offers the clearest evidence of what is possible. The cost of solar panels has fallen dramatically over the past decade, making new solar farms competitive with new fossil-fuel plants in many locations. Vietnam provides a striking example. After the government introduced generous feed-in tariffs — guaranteed prices paid for every unit of electricity fed into the grid — investors installed well over ten gigawatts of solar capacity within roughly two years, transforming a country with almost no solar power into a regional leader. Yet the boom also exposed a serious weakness. Transmission lines in the sunniest provinces could not carry all the electricity being produced, and grid operators were forced to order curtailment, instructing plants to reduce output even when the sun was shining. For investors who had expected to sell every kilowatt-hour, the losses were considerable.

Wind power presents a more mixed picture. Average wind speeds over much of the region's land are low, limiting onshore turbines to a few favourable areas. Offshore, however, conditions are considerably better, particularly along the coasts of Vietnam and the Philippines, where steady monsoon winds blow across wide, shallow continental shelves. Developing these sites is nonetheless far from straightforward. Turbines must be engineered to survive typhoons, specialised ports and vessels are needed for installation, and projects often take close to a decade to move from initial surveys to operation.

Whatever the mix of technologies, a power system that relies heavily on sun and wind must be able to cope with variability. Solar output disappears every evening, just as household demand peaks, and wind output can fall for days at a time. Most of the region's grids, however, were designed to distribute electricity from a small number of large, centralised power stations, not to balance thousands of small and intermittent generators. Three responses are commonly proposed. The first is to strengthen and digitise national grids so that electricity can be moved quickly from where it is generated to where it is needed. The second is cross-border interconnection: regional planners have long promoted an integrated ASEAN Power Grid, and some trade already takes place, with hydropower from Laos, for instance, exported to neighbouring countries. The third is storage, whether in large battery installations, which have become much cheaper recently, or in pumped hydro schemes that use surplus electricity to pump water uphill for release when demand rises.

Even where the technical solutions are clear, paying for them is not. Renewable projects are capital-intensive: almost all of their costs are incurred at the start, during construction, whereas the sunlight and wind they use are free. This makes them unusually sensitive to the cost of capital — the interest rates and returns that lenders and investors demand. In many developing economies, perceived risks such as currency fluctuations, uncertain regulation and the weak finances of state-owned utilities push this cost to two or three times the level in wealthy countries. As a result, an identical solar farm may produce considerably more expensive electricity in Manila or Jakarta than in Madrid. International initiatives such as the Just Energy Transition Partnerships agreed with Indonesia and Vietnam in 2022 aim to lower these costs by blending public and private money, although critics note that much of the promised funding consists of loans rather than grants.

A further complication is the region's existing fleet of coal-fired power stations. Unlike those in Europe or North America, many of these plants are less than fifteen years old and were financed on the assumption that they would operate for thirty or forty years. Many also operate under long-term contracts that oblige utilities to pay for their electricity whether or not it is needed. Retiring the plants early would turn them into stranded assets — investments that lose their value before the end of their expected lifetimes — and someone, whether owners, governments or consumers, would have to absorb the losses. Several proposed schemes would use low-cost international finance to buy out such plants and close them early, but the sums involved are large and the negotiations politically sensitive.

Finally, the transition must be fair if it is to be politically sustainable — the principle commonly described as a just transition. Coal-mining districts in Indonesia, for example, depend heavily on the industry for jobs and local government revenue, and closing mines without credible alternatives would provoke strong resistance. Renewable projects can create injustices of their own: large solar farms and hydropower dams require land, and communities that are displaced or lose access to rivers and forests rarely share in the benefits. Meaningful consultation, retraining for workers and protection for poorer households against sharp rises in electricity prices are therefore not optional extras but conditions for success.

Southeast Asia's energy future is not yet fixed. The falling cost of clean technologies gives the region a genuine opportunity to meet its growing demand without locking itself into decades of fossil-fuel dependence. Whether it seizes that opportunity will depend less on engineering breakthroughs than on decisions about grid investment, financial risk and the sharing of burdens — decisions that are, in the end, political.
